opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, after that summer I came away feeling that NLP wasn't really the direction I wanted to commit to. At the time, a lot of the work felt like it was about squeezing out small improvements on benchmarks: you'd tweak a model architecture, tune some hyperparameters, and get maybe half a point better on some dataset. It was hard for me to see where the deeper, more fundamental progress was coming from, and I didn't feel that excitement of "this is the thing I want to spend years on."

I think part of it was also the nature of the problems. Language felt kind of messy and hard to evaluate cleanly, and I often felt like I was fighting the data rather than understanding something. Compared to that, I was more drawn to areas where an agent actually interacts with an environment, where you can see behavior emerge and you get a clearer feedback signal. That's a big part of why I drifted toward reinforcement learning afterward.

Looking back, it's a little funny, because NLP turned out to be where so much of the action ended up with large language models. But I don't really regret it. That experience taught me what kind of research I personally enjoy, which is building systems, making things actually run well, and seeing tangible results. And in the end the paths sort of converged anyway, since RL became such an important part of training language models.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, that summer changed how I thought about it quite a bit. Before I went in, I had this image of NLP as kind of a separate world from what I was doing in reinforcement learning. Lots of linguistics, lots of hand-crafted pipelines, tokenizers and parsers and so on. I thought of it as a field with its own culture that I would probably never touch.

What I found when I actually worked on it was that the boundaries had mostly dissolved. The problems that mattered were about scale, about data, about training stability, about how you evaluate something that doesn't have a clean reward signal. Those are the same questions I was already asking in RL. The language part was almost the easy part. The hard part was engineering, and being honest with yourself about whether your model was actually doing what you claimed it was doing.

So I came out of it thinking NLP was less a research area in the traditional sense and more a testbed. It's where a lot of the general questions about learning get stress-tested first, because the data is enormous and the feedback from users is immediate. If something is wrong with your method, language will expose it very quickly.

The other thing that stuck with me was how much the field had become infrastructure-driven. A good idea without the systems to run it at scale doesn't go anywhere. That was a little humbling, but also motivating, because it meant the tooling work I enjoyed actually mattered to the science. I stopped seeing NLP as "somebody else's field" and started seeing it as a place where I could contribute from the angle I already knew.
